messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Since surviving a sudden, life-threatening illness eighteen months ago, Kwame Mensah, a 68-year-old widowed policy analyst, has lived as if the emergency never truly ended. He had been at his desk in a government office building, reviewing a budget brief, when a crushing wave of pain and dizziness came over him so fast that he could not make sense of what his body was doing. He remembered gripping the edge of the conference table, hearing chairs scrape back, and seeing a coworker’s mouth moving before the room blurred. In the ambulance and later in the hospital, what stayed with him was the terror of being trapped inside a body that seemed to turn against him without warning. Even after he was told he had survived, that moment never settled into something finished. Parts of it returned with a peculiar numbness, as if he were describing a stranger on a stretcher, but at other times the memory came with such force that he felt he was back under fluorescent hospital lights, overwhelmed and unable to keep thinking about it.

In the weeks after discharge, Kwame had come to believe that the illness had exposed something irreversible about him. What frightened him most was not only that he might die, but that his own body could no longer be counted on. He was certain now that his body was unreliable, an enemy capable of sounding an alarm at any moment, and he found himself watching it closely for signs of another collapse. That belief kept him tense through the day and night. He noticed every flutter in his chest, every spell of lightheadedness, every shift in his breathing, and even at home in his apartment he felt on guard, as if safety could be revoked without notice. He used to think of home as the one place where he could exhale after work; now he sat upright in the living room listening to his body, unable to settle.

His work as a policy analyst became one of the main places where this threat state showed itself. The ordinary setting of conference rooms, computer screens, and long stretches of concentrated reading had also been the setting of his medical crisis, and sitting through staff meetings could abruptly pull him back into the original moment. A colleague leaning across the table, the stale office air, or the pressure of trying to focus on a dense document could make the memory feel present rather than past. When that happened, his body tightened immediately, his attention narrowed, and he struggled to follow what was being discussed. Sometimes he would stare at the page and realize he had absorbed none of it because he was braced for danger again. The memory itself drove the sense of current threat; once it broke through, he was no longer a man in a meeting but someone in immediate peril.

Over time, the process also ran in the other direction. Because he stayed so alert to his body and surroundings, even minor internal sensations could cue the memory before he fully knew what was happening. A rush of tension in his chest while working at his desk, or the simple awareness that he was alone at home in the evening, could make the hospital scene surge back in fragments. He might first notice that he was suddenly rigid and scanning for danger, and only then find himself flooded with the image of the ambulance doors or the helpless certainty that something catastrophic was happening inside him again. On other occasions he could begin recalling the event in a flat, detached way, only for the emotion to slam into him so strongly that he had to stop and leave the thought unfinished.

As these episodes repeated, Kwame drew darker conclusions about what they meant. Each time his body leapt into alarm in a safe room, he took it as proof that something fundamental had been damaged. He had come to believe he would never feel normal emotions again, because his responses no longer seemed to match ordinary life; either he felt shut down and distant from what had happened, or he was overwhelmed by it. The constant tension and inability to concentrate seemed to confirm his view that his body was still reacting as if danger were ongoing and that he had no real control over it. That interpretation made him more watchful still, especially at home, and more convinced that another medical disaster could arrive without warning.

By the time he sought help, the strain had narrowed his life considerably. He still went to work, but tasks that once suited his careful, analytic mind now took much longer, and he had begun quietly declining some meetings because he feared freezing or losing focus in front of colleagues. Evenings in his apartment were the hardest; without distractions, he felt his body on alert and waited for it to betray him again. What finally brought him in was the sense that he was no longer living after the illness but remaining inside it. He said he wanted, more than anything, to feel that the event was over, but he was afraid that if he could not trust his own body, he would never again be able to feel safe, or fully himself.
